notes: Reasoning Ability part of BATCH_003: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) built by tools/batch_003/reasoning.py. New puzzle structures (a bench with distances, back-to-back rows, a row with ages, a hexagonal table with drinks, a square table with everyone facing the centre, an eight-seat rectangular table, a circle with ages and mixed facing, a ten-seat rectangular table with persons facing across, floors numbered from the top, a ground floor numbered 0, two persons per floor, a building of unknown height, three stacks of boxes, boxes holding counted items, months with colours, appointment dates with weekdays, a two-year month grid, a hobby week, designations with branches). Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding (inferred rules checked against alternative simple rules), series, alphabet, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items are hand-written. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Six persons on a bench, with distances
stimuli.content:
Six persons Gitanjali, Hridaan, Ishwari, Jasleen, Keshav and Lakshya sit on a long straight bench, all facing north. The gaps between neighbours are not all equal; distances are measured along the bench.

- Jasleen sits at the extreme left end of the bench.
- Keshav sits 7 m to the right of Jasleen, and exactly one person sits between them.
- Hridaan sits 3 m to the left of Keshav.
- Ishwari sits at the extreme right end of the bench, 13 m to the right of Keshav.
- Gitanjali sits 8 m to the left of Ishwari.
- Lakshya sits 2 m away from Gitanjali but not between Keshav and Gitanjali.
stimuli.solution:
Measure every position in metres east of Jasleen (the left end). Keshav = 7, and the one person between them is Hridaan at 7 − 3 = 4. Ishwari = 7 + 13 = 20 (the right end) and Gitanjali = 20 − 8 = 12. Lakshya is 2 m from Gitanjali: 10 lies between Keshav (7) and Gitanjali (12), so Lakshya = 14.

| Person | Metres east of Jasleen |
|---|---|
| Jasleen | 0 |
| Hridaan | 4 |
| Keshav | 7 |
| Gitanjali | 12 |
| Lakshya | 14 |
| Ishwari | 20 |

stimuli.title: Six friends at a hexagonal table, with drinks
stimuli.content:
Six friends Bhavesh, Chaitali, Dhaval, Eesha, Faraz and Hemlata sit around a hexagonal table, one at each side, all facing the centre. Each of them drinks a different one of Coffee, Juice, Lassi, Milk, Soup and Tea. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Dhaval sits opposite Bhavesh.
- Eesha sits immediately to the right of Bhavesh.
- Chaitali sits second to the right of Dhaval.
- Faraz sits immediately to the left of Chaitali.
- Bhavesh drinks Tea, and the person who drinks Coffee sits opposite him.
- The person who drinks Milk sits between Eesha and Dhaval.
- The person who drinks Lassi sits immediately to the right of the person who drinks Soup.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Bhavesh. Dhaval is opposite him, Eesha immediately to his right, Chaitali two places to Dhaval's right (immediately to Bhavesh's left) and Faraz between Dhaval and Chaitali. Hemlata takes the seat between Eesha and Dhaval. Bhavesh drinks Tea and Dhaval, opposite him, Coffee. The Milk drinker sits between Eesha and Dhaval: Hemlata. Of Eesha, Faraz and Chaitali, the only Soup–Lassi pair with Lassi immediately to the right is Faraz (Soup) and Chaitali (Lassi), so Eesha drinks Juice.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Bhavesh) | Person | Drink |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Bhavesh | Tea |
| 1 | Eesha | Juice |
| 2 | Hemlata | Milk |
| 3 | Dhaval | Coffee |
| 4 | Faraz | Soup |
| 5 | Chaitali | Lassi |

stimuli.title: Eight persons at a square table, all facing the centre
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kashish, Lalitha, Mukund, Neelam, Oorvi, Parveen, Raghu and Sanjana sit around a square table, all facing the centre. Four of them sit at the four corners and the other four at the middle of the four sides, so corner and middle seats alternate around the table.

- Kashish sits at one of the corners.
- Mukund sits opposite Kashish.
- Neelam sits second to the right of Kashish.
- Sanjana sits between Neelam and Mukund.
- Lalitha sits immediately to the left of Kashish.
- Parveen sits at a corner.
- Oorvi is not an immediate neighbour of Kashish.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Kashish at a corner. Mukund is opposite her (also a corner) and Neelam two seats to her right (a corner). Sanjana sits between Neelam and Mukund, and Lalitha immediately to Kashish's left (a middle seat). The seats left are the middle seat to Kashish's right, the middle seat after Mukund and the corner after it. Parveen takes the corner. Oorvi cannot be next to Kashish, so Oorvi takes the middle seat after Mukund and Raghu the middle seat to Kashish's right.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Kashish) | Person | Position |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Kashish | corner |
| 1 | Raghu | middle of a side |
| 2 | Neelam | corner |
| 3 | Sanjana | middle of a side |
| 4 | Mukund | corner |
| 5 | Oorvi | middle of a side |
| 6 | Parveen | corner |
| 7 | Lalitha | middle of a side |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a circle, with ages and mixed facing
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Anvesha, Bhairav, Chandrika, Dilnawaz, Evan, Ginni, Hussain and Ilina sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (For a person facing the centre the right is anticlockwise; for a person facing outside the right is clockwise.) Their ages are 22, 26, 31, 35, 40, 44, 49 and 53 years, one age each.

- Anvesha faces the centre, and Bhairav sits opposite her.
- Chandrika faces the centre and sits second to the right of Anvesha.
- Hussain, the youngest of the eight, sits between Anvesha and Chandrika and faces outside.
- Evan sits immediately to the right of Chandrika.
- Ilina sits second to the left of Evan.
- Dilnawaz sits immediately to the right of Ilina.
- Bhairav is 4 years older than Hussain.
- The oldest person sits second to the right of Anvesha.
- Only two persons are older than Ilina.
- Ginni is older than Anvesha.
- Evan is younger than Dilnawaz, and Dilnawaz is younger than Anvesha.
- Exactly four persons face the centre.
- Dilnawaz and Ginni face the same direction.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Anvesha (facing the centre); Bhairav is opposite her and Chandrika two seats anticlockwise, with Hussain (22, facing outside) between them. Chandrika faces the centre, so Evan is the next seat anticlockwise. If Evan faced the centre, second to his left (clockwise) would be Chandrika's seat, so Evan faces outside and Ilina sits two seats anticlockwise from him, next to Bhairav. If Ilina faced outside, the seat to her right would be Bhairav's, so Ilina faces the centre and Dilnawaz sits next to her; Ginni takes the last seat, beside Anvesha. Anvesha, Chandrika and Ilina face the centre; exactly one more does, and Dilnawaz and Ginni face the same way, so both face outside and Bhairav faces the centre. Ages: Bhairav 26, Chandrika (second to Anvesha's right) 53, Ilina 44. Ginni, Anvesha, Dilnawaz and Evan share 31, 35, 40 and 49 with Ginni > Anvesha > Dilnawaz > Evan.

| Seat (anticlockwise from Anvesha) | Person | Faces | Age |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anvesha | centre | 40 |
| 1 | Hussain | outside | 22 |
| 2 | Chandrika | centre | 53 |
| 3 | Evan | outside | 31 |
| 4 | Bhairav | centre | 26 |
| 5 | Ilina | centre | 44 |
| 6 | Dilnawaz | outside | 35 |
| 7 | Ginni | outside | 49 |

stimuli.title: A circle of unknown size
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. The number of persons is not given. Jharna, Kuber, Lajwanti, Mrinal, Nishit and Paromita are among them; the others are not named.

- Kuber sits third to the right of Jharna.
- Only five persons sit between Jharna and Kuber when counted to the left of Jharna.
- Lajwanti sits second to the left of Kuber.
- Only two persons sit between Mrinal and Kuber.
- Nishit sits immediately to the left of Jharna.
- Paromita sits immediately to the right of Kuber.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions anticlockwise (to the right) from Jharna = 0. Kuber = 3, with two persons between them on Jharna's right. Five persons sit between them on Jharna's left, so the circle has 2 + 5 + 2 = 9 persons. Lajwanti = 3 − 2 = 1, Paromita = 4 and Nishit = 8 (immediately to Jharna's left). Mrinal is three places from Kuber: 6 or 0; 0 is Jharna, so Mrinal = 6. Positions 2, 5 and 7 hold unnamed persons.

| Position (anticlockwise from Jharna) | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Jharna |
| 1 | Lajwanti |
| 2 | an unnamed person |
| 3 | Kuber |
| 4 | Paromita |
| 5 | an unnamed person |
| 6 | Mrinal |
| 7 | an unnamed person |
| 8 | Nishit |

stimuli.title: Seven persons from the ground floor up
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Bilal, Chhaya, Damodar, Esther, Gurleen, Harsha and Jeevika live in a building that has a ground floor and six floors above it. The ground floor is numbered 0 and the topmost floor 6; one person lives on each floor. Each person works in a different city among Agra, Bhopal, Kochi, Nagpur, Patna, Surat and Thane.

- Damodar lives on floor 3 and works in Patna.
- Only two persons live between Damodar and the person who works in Kochi, who lives above Damodar.
- Esther works in Kochi.
- Harsha lives on the ground floor.
- The person who works in Surat lives immediately below Esther.
- Bilal and Chhaya live on odd-numbered floors, and Bilal lives above Chhaya.
- Gurleen lives immediately above the person who works in Bhopal.
- The person who works in Thane lives between Chhaya and Damodar.
- Jeevika does not work in Nagpur.
stimuli.solution:
Damodar = 3 (Patna); the Kochi worker, Esther, lives three floors higher: 6. The Surat worker lives on floor 5. Harsha = 0. Bilal and Chhaya take odd floors other than 3 with Bilal higher: Bilal = 5 (Surat) and Chhaya = 1. Floors 2 and 4 remain for Gurleen and Jeevika. Gurleen is immediately above the Bhopal worker: Gurleen = 4 would make Damodar (Patna) the Bhopal worker, so Gurleen = 2, Chhaya works in Bhopal and Jeevika = 4. The Thane worker lives between Chhaya (1) and Damodar (3): Gurleen. Jeevika does not work in Nagpur, so Jeevika works in Agra and Harsha in Nagpur.

| Floor | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Esther | Kochi |
| 5 | Bilal | Surat |
| 4 | Jeevika | Agra |
| 3 | Damodar | Patna |
| 2 | Gurleen | Thane |
| 1 | Chhaya | Bhopal |
| 0 | Harsha | Nagpur |

stimuli.title: Eight persons, two on each of four floors
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kavita, Manish, Natasha, Pallav, Ronak, Shalini, Uttam and Vibha live in a four-storey building, two persons on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 4 the topmost.

- Kavita lives on an odd-numbered floor, and Ronak lives on the floor immediately below Kavita's floor.
- Manish lives on the topmost floor.
- Natasha lives on the same floor as Ronak.
- Pallav lives on a floor below Natasha's floor.
- Shalini lives neither on Kavita's floor nor on Manish's floor.
- Uttam lives on a floor above Shalini's floor but below Vibha's floor.
- Exactly two persons live on each floor.
stimuli.solution:
Kavita is on an odd floor with Ronak one floor below, so Kavita = 3 and Ronak = 2 (Kavita = 1 leaves no floor below). Manish = 4. Natasha joins Ronak on floor 2, which is now full, and Pallav lives below it: floor 1. Shalini avoids floors 3 and 4, so she is on floor 1. Uttam lives between Shalini and Vibha: one place is left on floor 3 and one on floor 4, so Uttam = 3 and Vibha = 4.

| Floor | Persons |
|---|---|
| 4 | Manish and Vibha |
| 3 | Kavita and Uttam |
| 2 | Natasha and Ronak |
| 1 | Pallav and Shalini |

stimuli.title: A building of unknown height
stimuli.content:
Some persons live in a building, one person on each floor; every floor is occupied. Floor 1 is the lowermost. The number of floors is not given. Aarush, Bhoomika, Chakor, Devika, Ekansh and Fiona live in the building; the other residents are not named.

- Chakor lives on floor 4.
- Only three persons live between Chakor and Devika, and Devika lives above Chakor.
- Aarush lives on the topmost floor, and only five persons live between Aarush and Devika.
- Ekansh lives exactly midway between Chakor and Aarush.
- Fiona lives as many floors below Chakor as Ekansh lives above Devika.
- Only two persons live between Bhoomika and Aarush.
stimuli.solution:
Chakor = 4, so Devika = 8. Aarush is six floors from Devika and lives on the top floor, so Aarush = 14 (2 is below Devika and cannot be the top): the building has 14 floors. Ekansh = (4 + 14) ÷ 2 = 9, one floor above Devika, so Fiona is one floor below Chakor: 3. Bhoomika is three floors from Aarush: 11.

| Floor | Person |
|---|---|
| 14 | Aarush |
| 11 | Bhoomika |
| 9 | Ekansh |
| 8 | Devika |
| 4 | Chakor |
| 3 | Fiona |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in three stacks
stimuli.content:
Nine boxes B, D, G, K, M, P, S, V and X are kept in three stacks, left, middle and right, with three boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 3 its top.

- Box V is at level 2 of the middle stack.
- Box D is placed directly above box V.
- Box K is at the bottom of the stack that holds box D.
- Box G is at the bottom of the right stack.
- Box P is at the same level as box V but not in the same stack as box B.
- Box B is placed directly below box X.
- Box S is at the bottom of its stack.
- Box S is not in the same stack as box M.
stimuli.solution:
Middle stack: K (bottom), V, D. G is at the bottom of the right stack, so S, also at a bottom, is at the bottom of the left stack. P is at level 2 of the left or right stack. If P were in the left stack, B (not in P's stack) would have to be in the right stack with X above it: B at level 2, X at level 3; then M would join S in the left stack, which is not allowed. So P is at level 2 of the right stack, B and X fill levels 2 and 3 of the left stack, and M tops the right stack.

| Level | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | X | D | M |
| 2 | B | V | P |
| 1 | S | K | G |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes in four colours
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes C, E, H, J, L, N, R and T are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom, 8 the top). Each box is Blue, Green, Red or White, and exactly two boxes are of each colour.

- Box T is placed fourth from the bottom and is blue.
- The other blue box is at the top of the stack.
- Each green box is placed immediately below a blue box.
- Box L is placed immediately above box T.
- Box C is green and is placed above box L.
- Box J is at the bottom and is red.
- Exactly two boxes are placed between the two white boxes.
- Box E is green.
- Box N is placed below box R, and box H is blue.
stimuli.solution:
Blue boxes: T (4) and the top box (8). The green boxes sit just below them: positions 3 and 7. L = 5. C is green and above L, so C = 7; E, the other green box, = 3. J = 1 (red). Positions 2, 5 and 6 hold one red and two white boxes; the whites have two boxes between them, so they are at 2 and 5 and position 6 is red. H is blue, so H = 8; N below R puts N at 2 and R at 6.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | H | Blue |
| 7 | C | Green |
| 6 | R | Red |
| 5 | L | White |
| 4 | T | Blue |
| 3 | E | Green |
| 2 | N | White |
| 1 | J | Red |

stimuli.title: Seven workshops from April to October, with colours
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anaya, Bodhi, Chinmayi, Daivik, Eila, Girik and Hiral attend a workshop, one person in each month from April to October of the same year. Each of them likes a different colour among Blue, Green, Maroon, Orange, Pink, White and Yellow.

- Chinmayi's workshop is in a month that has 31 days, and only two workshops are held after hers.
- The person who likes White attends two months before Chinmayi.
- Girik attends in the month immediately after the person who likes White.
- Eila attends in the month immediately after Chinmayi, and Bodhi attends after Eila.
- Daivik attends before Hiral, and neither of them likes White.
- The person who likes Maroon attends in the last month.
- Chinmayi likes Green, and the person who likes Yellow attends immediately before her.
- Hiral likes neither Pink nor Orange, and Eila does not like Pink.
stimuli.solution:
Two workshops come after Chinmayi's, so hers is in August (31 days). White is two months earlier: June; Girik follows in July. Eila is in September and Bodhi, after her, in October. April, May and June remain for Anaya, Daivik and Hiral; Daivik and Hiral do not like White, so Anaya is in June and Daivik (April) is before Hiral (May). Chinmayi likes Green and Girik (July) Yellow; Bodhi (October) likes Maroon. Blue, Orange and Pink remain for Daivik, Hiral and Eila: Hiral takes Blue, and Eila, not Pink, takes Orange; Daivik likes Pink.

| Month | Person | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| April | Daivik | Pink |
| May | Hiral | Blue |
| June | Anaya | White |
| July | Girik | Yellow |
| August | Chinmayi | Green |
| September | Eila | Orange |
| October | Bodhi | Maroon |

stimuli.title: Six appointments in a month that starts on a Monday
stimuli.content:
Six customers Nirmal, Oishi, Pavan, Rasika, Shubh and Vedika each have one appointment at a bank in the same month, on six different dates. The month has 30 days, and its 1st is a Monday.

- Oishi's appointment is on the second Wednesday of the month.
- Nirmal's appointment is exactly one week before Oishi's.
- Shubh's appointment is on the fourth Monday of the month.
- Rasika's appointment is on a Friday before Shubh's.
- Pavan's appointment is on a Sunday, after Oishi's but before Rasika's.
- Vedika's appointment is on the last Saturday of the month.
stimuli.solution:
Mondays fall on 1, 8, 15, 22, 29; Wednesdays on 3, 10, 17, 24; Fridays on 5, 12, 19, 26; Saturdays on 6, 13, 20, 27; Sundays on 7, 14, 21, 28. Oishi = 10 (second Wednesday), Nirmal = 3, Shubh = 22 (fourth Monday), Vedika = 27 (last Saturday). Rasika is on a Friday before the 22nd: 5, 12 or 19, and a Sunday (Pavan) must fit between the 10th and Rasika's date, so Rasika = 19 and Pavan = 14.

| Customer | Date | Day |
|---|---|---|
| Nirmal | 3 | Wednesday |
| Oishi | 10 | Wednesday |
| Pavan | 14 | Sunday |
| Rasika | 19 | Friday |
| Shubh | 22 | Monday |
| Vedika | 27 | Saturday |

stimuli.title: Eight officers joining over two years
stimuli.content:
Eight officers Aadya, Bhavin, Darpan, Eshwari, Gyan, Hetal, Jagrut and Kirtana joined a bank. Each joined in a different one of these eight months: March, June, September and December of 2024, and March, June, September and December of 2025.

- Bhavin joined in June of one of the two years.
- Only three persons joined between Bhavin and Darpan, and Darpan joined before Bhavin.
- Aadya joined in December of the year in which Darpan joined.
- Eshwari joined immediately after Bhavin, and Gyan joined after Eshwari.
- Hetal joined before Kirtana, and both of them joined in the same year.
stimuli.solution:
List the eight months in time order (Mar 24, Jun 24, Sep 24, Dec 24, Mar 25, Jun 25, Sep 25, Dec 25). Bhavin joined in a June and Darpan four places earlier, so Bhavin = June 2025 and Darpan = June 2024. Aadya = December 2024. Eshwari = September 2025 and Gyan, after her, = December 2025. March 2024, September 2024 and March 2025 remain; Hetal and Kirtana joined in the same year with Hetal first, so Hetal = March 2024, Kirtana = September 2024 and Jagrut = March 2025.

| Month | Officer |
|---|---|
| March 2024 | Hetal |
| June 2024 | Darpan |
| September 2024 | Kirtana |
| December 2024 | Aadya |
| March 2025 | Jagrut |
| June 2025 | Bhavin |

stimuli.title: Seven hobby classes in a week
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abeer, Brinda, Darius, Elora, Gauransh, Ivaan and Mehr each attend one hobby class in the same week, one class on each day from Monday to Sunday. The classes are Chess, Cooking, Dance, Music, Painting, Pottery and Yoga, one each.

- Mehr's class is exactly in the middle of the week.
- Only two classes are held between Mehr's class and the Cooking class, which is held after Mehr's.
- The Dance class is held on Friday.
- Abeer attends the Music class, which is held two days before the Dance class.
- Elora attends on Monday, and Gauransh attends the Chess class.
- Darius attends on the day immediately before Brinda.
- Ivaan attends after Darius, but not on Saturday.
- Mehr attends neither Painting nor Yoga, and Brinda does not attend Yoga.
stimuli.solution:
Mehr = Thursday, Cooking = Sunday, Dance = Friday, and Music (Abeer) = Wednesday. Elora = Monday. Tuesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday remain for Brinda, Darius, Gauransh and Ivaan. Darius–Brinda are consecutive: Friday–Saturday (Saturday–Sunday would leave no later day for Ivaan). Ivaan = Sunday (Cooking) and Gauransh = Tuesday (Chess); Darius takes Dance. Of Painting, Pottery and Yoga, Mehr takes Pottery, Brinda Painting and Elora Yoga.

| Day | Person | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Elora | Yoga |
| Tuesday | Gauransh | Chess |
| Wednesday | Abeer | Music |
| Thursday | Mehr | Pottery |
| Friday | Darius | Dance |
| Saturday | Brinda | Painting |

stimuli.title: Six officers, designations and postings
stimuli.content:
Six officers Nikunj, Quresh, Rutvi, Saanvi, Tanush and Udit hold six different designations. In decreasing order of seniority the designations are: Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Director, Section Officer and Assistant. Each officer is posted in a different city among Indore, Jaipur, Lucknow, Mysuru, Ranchi and Shimla.

- Only two officers are senior to Nikunj.
- The officer posted in Jaipur is immediately junior to Nikunj, and Saanvi is posted in Jaipur.
- Tanush is junior to Quresh, who is junior to Saanvi.
- Rutvi is senior to Udit.
- The officer posted in Shimla is senior to the officer posted in Indore, and both are senior to Nikunj.
- The Assistant is posted in Lucknow.
- Quresh is not posted in Ranchi.
stimuli.solution:
Nikunj is third (Deputy Director) and Saanvi fourth (Assistant Director, Jaipur). Quresh and Tanush are junior to Saanvi: Section Officer and Assistant, in that order. Rutvi (Director) is senior to Udit (Joint Director). The Shimla and Indore officers are the two above Nikunj, Shimla first: Rutvi – Shimla, Udit – Indore. Tanush (Assistant) is in Lucknow. Mysuru and Ranchi remain for Nikunj and Quresh; Quresh is not in Ranchi, so Quresh – Mysuru and Nikunj – Ranchi.

| Designation | Officer | City |
|---|---|---|
| Director | Rutvi | Shimla |
| Joint Director | Udit | Indore |
| Deputy Director | Nikunj | Ranchi |
| Assistant Director | Saanvi | Jaipur |
| Section Officer | Quresh | Mysuru |
| Assistant | Tanush | Lucknow |

stimuli.title: Arrow codes for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode each symbol from left to right, draw the persons as a family tree (fathers, mothers, spouses, children) and read the asked relation off the tree. A person's gender follows from the relation they are given (father, son, husband: male; daughter, sister: female) or from their spouse.

stimuli.title: A three-generation family with professions
stimuli.content:
A family has seven members of three generations: Ramesh, Savita, Vikas, Anjali, Pooja, Dhruv and Kriti. Ramesh, Vikas and Dhruv are male; the others are female. Each member has a different profession among Banker, Doctor, Engineer, Lawyer, Pilot, Student and Teacher.

- Ramesh and Savita are married to each other; Vikas and Anjali are their only children.
- Pooja is the wife of Vikas, and Dhruv and Kriti are their children.
- The Lawyer and the Teacher are the two members of the oldest generation, and Savita is not the Lawyer.
- The Engineer is the father of the Banker.
- The Doctor is the daughter-in-law of the Teacher.
- The Student is the brother of the Banker.
stimuli.solution:
Ramesh is the Lawyer and Savita the Teacher. Savita's only daughter-in-law is Pooja: the Doctor. The Engineer is a father, and the only father outside the oldest generation is Vikas, so Vikas is the Engineer and the Banker is Dhruv or Kriti. The Student is the Banker's brother, so the Banker is Kriti and the Student Dhruv. Anjali is the Pilot.

| Member | Relation | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| Ramesh | grandfather | Lawyer |
| Savita | grandmother | Teacher |
| Vikas | son of Ramesh and Savita | Engineer |
| Anjali | daughter of Ramesh and Savita | Pilot |
| Pooja | wife of Vikas | Doctor |
| Dhruv | son of Vikas and Pooja | Student |
| Kriti | daughter of Vikas and Pooja | Banker |

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about farming
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'green fields need rain' is written as 'ka mo zi lu'
'rain helps the crops' is written as 'zi pe ra ne'
'crops need care' is written as 'ne mo fa'
'care for green fields' is written as 'fa ka lu bo'

(The codes of the words in a sentence may appear in any order.)
stimuli.solution: need = mo (sentences 1 and 3); rain = zi (sentences 1 and 2); crops = ne (sentences 2 and 3); care = fa (sentences 3 and 4); green and fields share {ka, lu} (sentences 1 and 4) and cannot be told apart; for = bo (sentence 4); helps and the share {pe, ra}.

stimuli.title: Coding by word length, then vowels
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language, each word is coded by the steps below.
Step 1: If the word has an even number of letters, its first half and second half are interchanged. If the word has an odd number of letters, its middle letter is replaced by the number of letters in the word.
Step 2: Every vowel (A, E, I, O, U) in the result of Step 1 is replaced by the letter that comes immediately after it in the English alphabet.

Each question gives a word; choose its code.
stimuli.solution: Count the letters first (even: swap the halves; odd: replace the middle letter by the count), then move every remaining vowel one step forward. Consonants and the inserted number do not change in Step 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Mehul, Nandini, Omisha, Pritam, Rashmi and Sudeep sit in a straight row, all facing north.
- Rashmi sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Pritam sits third to the right of Rashmi.
- Only one person sits between Pritam and Nandini.
- Mehul sits immediately to the left of Nandini.
- Omisha is not an immediate neighbour of Rashmi.

Who sits second to the left of Pritam?

solution.concept: Facing north: the right is towards the east, the left towards the west
solution.explanation: Rashmi must be at the left end (from the right end there is no room for Pritam three seats to her right), so Rashmi = 1 and Pritam = 4. Nandini is two seats from Pritam: seat 2 or 6. Seat 2 would put Mehul at seat 1, Rashmi's seat, so Nandini = 6 and Mehul = 5. Omisha cannot sit next to Rashmi, so Omisha = 3 and Sudeep = 2. Second to Pritam's left is seat 2: Sudeep.
steps: Rashmi at the right end leaves no seat three places to her right ⇒ Rashmi = 1, Pritam = 4
Nandini = 2 or 6; Nandini = 2 needs Mehul at 1 (taken) ⇒ Nandini = 6, Mehul = 5
Omisha not next to Rashmi ⇒ Omisha = 3, Sudeep = 2
Left to right: Rashmi, Sudeep, Omisha, Pritam, Mehul, Nandini; second to the left of Pritam (4) = seat 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Omisha is immediately to Pritam's left; Mehul is immediately to his right; Rashmi is third to his left.

East of Keshav: Gitanjali (12), Lakshya (14), Ishwari (20)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Amrita, Baldev, Charu, Dushyant, Eeshan, Gargi, Himesh and Indira sit in two rows of four seats each. The rows are placed back to back: the persons in Row 1 face north and those in Row 2 face south, and each seat of Row 1 is directly back to back with one seat of Row 2.
- Charu sits at an extreme end of Row 1.
- Amrita sits second to the left of Charu.
- Himesh sits immediately to the right of Amrita.
- Baldev sits back to back with Himesh.
- Indira sits immediately to the right of Baldev.
- Eeshan faces south and sits back to back with Gargi.

Who sits back to back with the person who sits immediately to the left of Indira?

solution.concept: Back-to-back rows: 'right' points in opposite directions in the two rows
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 4 from west to east in both rows. Charu is at an end of Row 1, and Amrita is two seats to her left (west), so Charu = seat 4 and Amrita = seat 2; Himesh is immediately to Amrita's right: seat 3. Baldev is behind Himesh in Row 2, seat 3. Baldev faces south, so his right is west: Indira = Row 2, seat 2. Eeshan (Row 2) and Gargi are back to back in the only fully free column, seat 1, and Dushyant takes Row 2, seat 4. Indira faces south, so her left is east: Baldev. The person back to back with Baldev is Himesh.
steps: Row 1 (facing north): Charu = 4 (at seat 1 there is no seat two places to her left), Amrita = 2, Himesh = 3
Row 2 (facing south): Baldev = 3 (behind Himesh), Indira = 2 (to Baldev's right = west)
Column 1: Gargi (Row 1) and Eeshan (Row 2); Dushyant = Row 2, seat 4
Immediately to Indira's left (east) = Baldev; back to back with Baldev = Himesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Amrita is back to back with Indira herself; Charu is back to back with Dushyant; Dushyant is in Row 2, so he is not back to back with anyone in his own row.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Jagdish, Kamini, Manoj, Nalini, Prerna, Qamar and Rohini sit in a straight row, all facing north. Their ages are 21, 25, 29, 33, 37, 41 and 45 years, one age each.
- Manoj sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Only one person sits between Manoj and the oldest person.
- The youngest person sits immediately to the right of the oldest person.
- Nalini sits at the extreme right end and is 4 years older than the youngest person.
- Jagdish sits immediately to the left of Nalini and is older than Manoj.
- Prerna is 29 years old and sits to the right of Manoj.
- Qamar is older than Prerna but younger than Manoj.
- Qamar sits at an extreme end of the row, and Rohini is not the oldest.

What is the sum of the ages of the two persons who sit at the extreme ends of the row?

solution.concept: Seating combined with an age ranking
solution.explanation: Manoj = 4, Nalini = 7, Jagdish = 6, and Prerna (to Manoj's right) = 5; Qamar takes an end, so Qamar = 1. The oldest sits at 2 or 6. If at 6, the youngest would be Nalini at 7, but Nalini is 4 years older than the youngest: rejected. So the oldest is at 2 and the youngest at 3. Rohini is not the oldest, so Rohini = 3 (21) and Kamini = 2 (45); Nalini = 25. Qamar, Manoj and Jagdish share 33, 37, 41 with Prerna (29) < Qamar < Manoj < Jagdish: Qamar 33, Manoj 37, Jagdish 41. The ends are Qamar (33) and Nalini (25): 58.
steps: Seats: Manoj 4, Nalini 7, Jagdish 6, Prerna 5, Qamar 1
Oldest at 6 would make Nalini the youngest, contradicting 'Nalini = youngest + 4' ⇒ oldest at 2, youngest at 3
Rohini not oldest ⇒ Rohini 3 (21), Kamini 2 (45); Nalini 21 + 4 = 25
29 < Qamar < Manoj < Jagdish ⇒ 33, 37, 41
Ends: Qamar 33 + Nalini 25 = 58
solution.why_others_wrong: 62 and 66 come from putting Kamini or Rohini at the left end; 54 uses Qamar's age as 29.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Abhay, Bushra, Cyril, Daksha, Elvin, Feroze, Gulshan and Hansa sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre.
- Gulshan sits opposite Abhay.
- Hansa sits second to the right of Abhay.
- Only two persons sit between Hansa and Feroze when counted to the left of Hansa.
- Cyril sits immediately to the left of Gulshan.
- Elvin sits immediately to the right of Abhay.
- Bushra is not an immediate neighbour of Feroze.

Who sits third to the left of the person who sits second to the right of Feroze?

solution.concept: Two-step position questions
solution.explanation: Number the seats anticlockwise from Abhay (0); facing the centre, right = anticlockwise. Gulshan = 4, Hansa = 2, Elvin = 1, Cyril = 3 (immediately to Gulshan's left, i.e. clockwise). Two persons between Hansa and Feroze on Hansa's left (clockwise: Elvin, Abhay) puts Feroze at 7. Bushra cannot be next to Feroze, so Bushra = 5 and Daksha = 6. Second to Feroze's right is Elvin (seat 1); third to Elvin's left (clockwise) is seat 6: Daksha.
steps: Abhay 0, Elvin 1, Hansa 2, Gulshan 4, Cyril 3
Clockwise from Hansa: Elvin, Abhay, then Feroze ⇒ Feroze 7
Bushra not beside Feroze ⇒ Bushra 5, Daksha 6
Second to the right of Feroze (7 + 2 = 1): Elvin
Third to the left of Elvin (1 − 3 = 6): Daksha
solution.why_others_wrong: Bushra is third to the left of Abhay; Abhay is the person immediately to Elvin's left; Hansa is immediately to Elvin's right.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Jayant, Kesari, Leher, Mitali, Nayana, Owais, Pankhuri and Ruchir sit around a rectangular table, all facing the centre. One person sits at each of the two shorter sides and three persons sit along each of the two longer sides; each person on a longer side sits directly across the table from one person on the other longer side.
- Jayant and Nayana sit at the two shorter sides.
- Mitali sits second to the right of Jayant.
- Ruchir sits immediately to the right of Mitali.
- Kesari sits directly across the table from Mitali.
- Owais sits immediately to the right of Nayana.
- Leher sits immediately to the right of Jayant.

Who sits directly across the table from Owais?

solution.concept: Rectangular table: 'across' pairs the seats of the two longer sides
solution.explanation: Going right (anticlockwise) from Jayant: Leher, Mitali and Ruchir fill the first longer side, then Nayana at the other shorter side, then Owais, Kesari and Pankhuri on the second longer side. Kesari is across from Mitali (the two middle seats). Owais is the first seat after Nayana, which is across from the last seat before Nayana: Ruchir.
steps: Jayant (short side); Leher, Mitali, Ruchir on long side 1
Nayana (other short side); Owais next to her
Kesari across from Mitali (middle of long side 2); Pankhuri takes the last seat
Across pairs: Leher–Pankhuri, Mitali–Kesari, Ruchir–Owais
solution.why_others_wrong: Leher is across from Pankhuri and Mitali from Kesari; Kesari sits beside Owais.

steps: Anticlockwise from Anvesha: Anvesha (centre, 40), Hussain (outside, 22), Chandrika (centre, 53), Evan (outside, 31), Bhairav (centre, 26), Ilina (centre, 44), Dilnawaz (outside, 35), Ginni (outside, 49)
Dilnawaz = 35
Opposite Dilnawaz (seat 6): seat 2 = Chandrika

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the position of Nishit with respect to Mrinal?

steps: 9 persons; anticlockwise from Jharna: Jharna, Lajwanti, an unnamed person, Kuber, Paromita, an unnamed person, Mrinal, an unnamed person, Nishit
From Mrinal (6), right = anticlockwise: 7 (unnamed), 8 (Nishit)
solution.why_others_wrong: Going left (clockwise) from Mrinal, Nishit is seventh, not second.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Gopika, Harmeet, Kanha, Laxmi and Tejal live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor. The floors are numbered from the top: floor 1 is the topmost floor and floor 5 the lowermost.
- Kanha lives on floor 4.
- Tejal lives on the floor immediately above Kanha's floor.
- Only one person lives between Tejal and Gopika.
- Gopika lives below Kanha.
- Laxmi lives above Harmeet.

Who lives on floor 2?

solution.concept: Read the numbering: here a smaller floor number is higher up
solution.explanation: Floor 1 is the top. Kanha = 4 and Tejal, immediately above, = 3. Gopika is two floors from Tejal and below Kanha, so Gopika = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain; Laxmi lives above Harmeet, so Laxmi = 1 and Harmeet = 2.
steps: Kanha 4; 'immediately above' means one number smaller ⇒ Tejal 3
Gopika = 3 ± 2 and below Kanha ⇒ 5
Laxmi above Harmeet ⇒ Laxmi 1 (top), Harmeet 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Tejal is on floor 3; Laxmi on floor 1; Kanha on floor 4. Reading floor 1 as the bottom would reverse the order.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Darsh, Elakshi, Mahima, Rudraksh and Saket live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Each owns a different pet among Cat, Dog, Fish, Parrot and Rabbit.
- Rudraksh lives on the topmost floor and owns the Parrot.
- Only one person lives between Rudraksh and Darsh.
- Elakshi lives immediately above Darsh.
- Mahima lives below Saket.
- The person who owns the Cat lives on floor 3.
- The person who owns the Dog lives immediately above the person who owns the Fish.

Who owns the Rabbit?

solution.concept: Floors first, then the attribute
solution.explanation: Rudraksh = 5, so Darsh = 3 and Elakshi = 4; Mahima below Saket gives Mahima = 1 and Saket = 2. Darsh (floor 3) owns the Cat. The Dog–Fish pair needs two adjacent floors without the Cat or the Parrot: floors 2 and 1, so Saket owns the Dog and Mahima the Fish. Elakshi owns the Rabbit.
steps: Rudraksh 5 (Parrot) ⇒ Darsh 3, Elakshi 4
Mahima 1, Saket 2
Cat on floor 3 = Darsh
Dog immediately above Fish: only floors 2–1 are free of Cat and Parrot ⇒ Saket Dog, Mahima Fish
Remaining: Elakshi – Rabbit
solution.why_others_wrong: Darsh owns the Cat, Saket the Dog and Mahima the Fish.

Agra: Jeevika (4) ⇒ floor 5: Bilal

Floor 2: Gurleen; floor 4: Jeevika

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which city does Harsha work?

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true?

solution.explanation: Gurleen lives on floor 2. Chhaya works in Bhopal, Jeevika (not Bilal) lives immediately above Damodar, and only Bilal lives between Esther and Jeevika.
steps: Ground floor (0) to floor 6: Harsha (Nagpur), Chhaya (Bhopal), Gurleen (Thane), Damodar (Patna), Jeevika (Agra), Bilal (Surat), Esther (Kochi)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who lives on the same floor as Uttam?

solution.concept: Floors that hold two persons
solution.explanation: Floor 3 has room for one person besides Kavita, and Uttam must be above Shalini (floor 1) and below Vibha, so he is on floor 3 with Kavita.
steps: Floor 4: Manish and Vibha; Floor 3: Kavita and Uttam; Floor 2: Natasha and Ronak; Floor 1: Pallav and Shalini

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: On which floor does Natasha live?

steps: Floor 4: Manish and Vibha; Floor 3: Kavita and Uttam; Floor 2: Natasha and Ronak; Floor 1: Pallav and Shalini

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

questions.question_text:
Six boxes B, F, K, Q, W and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom, 6 the top). Their weights are 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 20 kg, one weight per box.
- The heaviest box is placed third from the bottom.
- Box W is placed immediately below the heaviest box, and box F immediately above it.
- Box F weighs 3 kg less than box W.
- Box K weighs 8 kg and is placed above box Q.
- The weights of the top box and the bottom box add up to 19 kg.
- Box Y is heavier than box Q, and box B is placed above box Q.

By how many kilograms is box W heavier than box B?

solution.concept: Weights and positions solved together
solution.explanation: W = 2, the 20 kg box = 3, F = 4. K weighs 8 kg; F = W − 3, so (W, F) is (17, 14), (14, 11) or (11, 8), and the last fails because 8 kg is K's. The two ends add to 19: 8 + 11 or 5 + 14. If (W, F) = (14, 11), both pairs need a weight already used by W or F, so W = 17 and F = 14. Now 5 + 14 is impossible too, so the ends are K (8 kg) and an 11 kg box; K is above Q, so K cannot be at the bottom: K is on top and the 11 kg box at the bottom. B, Q and Y share position 1 (11 kg), 3 (20 kg) and 5 (5 kg). B is above Q, so Q is not at 5; Y is heavier than Q, so Q is not the 20 kg box: Q = 1 (11 kg). Then Y = 20 kg at position 3 and B = 5 kg at position 5. W − B = 17 − 5 = 12 kg.
steps: W at 2, heaviest (20 kg) at 3, F at 4
Ends sum to 19: only K (8) on top + an 11 kg box at the bottom works, and it needs W = 17, F = 14
B above Q and Y heavier than Q ⇒ Q = bottom (11 kg), Y = 20 kg (position 3), B = 5 kg (position 5)
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 kg is W − K; 3 kg is W − F; 6 kg is Q − B.

Either conclusion I or II follows

I alone is not certain; II alone is not certain
I and II are complementary (same subject and predicate) ⇒ Either I or II follows

solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.question_text: Introducing a boy, Sunita said, "His father is the only son of my mother." How is Sunita related to the boy?

Boy's father = Sunita's brother
Father's sister = aunt (paternal aunt)
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother would need Sunita to be the boy's parent, but his father is her brother; sister would need the same father for both.

solution.explanation: R is Q's father and S is R's daughter, so S is Q's sister. P is Q's wife, so S is P's husband's sister: her sister-in-law.
steps: R is Q's father; S is R's daughter ⇒ S is Q's sister
P is Q's wife
Husband's sister ⇒ sister-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother-in-law would be R's wife; S is not P's own sister or daughter.

solution.explanation: Rakesh is a son of his own father, and his father has only one son, so that only son is Rakesh. Tanvi's father is therefore Rakesh.
steps: Rakesh's father's sons include Rakesh
'Only son' ⇒ the only son is Rakesh
Tanvi's father = Rakesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Uncle would need Rakesh's father to have a second son; grandfather and brother ignore the word 'only'.

questions.question_text: If 'P ↑ Q → R ↓ S', how is P related to S?

solution.concept: Two parents of the same child
solution.explanation: P is Q's father; Q is R's sister, so P is R's father too. R is S's daughter, so S is R's other parent. Since P is the father, S is the mother, and P is S's husband.
steps: P ↑ Q: P is Q's father
Q → R: Q and R are sisters ⇒ P is R's father
R ↓ S: S is R's parent ⇒ S is the mother
P is S's husband
solution.why_others_wrong: Father would make S P's child, but S is a parent of P's daughter R.

solution.concept: Mother's sibling's relation to the child
solution.explanation: J is K's son and K is L's husband, so L is J's mother. L is M's sister, so M is J's mother's sibling, and J is M's nephew.
steps: J ↔ K: J is K's son
K ← L: K is L's husband ⇒ L is J's mother
L → M: L is M's sister
J = son of M's sister ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Cousin is J's relation to M's children; brother-in-law is K's relation to M.

solution.explanation: U is V's sister; V is W's father; W is X's son, so X is W's other parent, i.e. V's wife. U is the sister of X's husband: X's sister-in-law.
steps: U → V: U is V's sister
V ↑ W: V is W's father
W ↔ X: X is W's parent ⇒ X is V's wife
Husband's sister ⇒ sister-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt is U's relation to W, not to X; mother-in-law would be V's mother.

A ↑ B ↓ C ⇒ A is C's husband

questions.question_text: Rakesh walks 9 m towards the south. He then turns left and walks 12 m, and then turns left again and walks 4 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement with a 5-12-13 triangle
solution.explanation: Left from south is east, and left from east is north. He ends 12 m east and 9 − 4 = 5 m south of the start: √(144 + 25) = 13 m, towards the south-east.
steps: 9 m south → (0, −9)
Left from south = east; 12 m → (12, −9)
Left from east = north; 4 m → (12, −5)
√(12² + 5²) = 13 m; east and south ⇒ South-East
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West mixes up the first left turn; 25 m adds the legs; North-East ignores that he is still south of the start.

West on his left ⇒ facing north
Two right turns: north → east → south
Facing south, west is to the right ⇒ shadow to his right
solution.why_others_wrong: 'To his left' ignores the turns; a shadow falls behind or in front only when facing east or west.

I. A software company in the city reported a record profit this quarter.
II. The city's traffic police introduced a one-way system in the business district this quarter.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: A company's profit results from its business performance, and a traffic plan from the police's assessment of congestion. Neither explains the other and no single event explains both: they are effects of independent causes.
steps: I: outcome of the company's business
II: outcome of a traffic decision
No link and no shared trigger ⇒ effects of independent causes
solution.why_others_wrong: A common cause would need one event driving both a company's profit and a traffic rule; nothing suggests one.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Many students of a village school drop out after Class 8 because the nearest school that teaches Classes 9 and 10 is 15 km away and there is no bus.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Provide free transport to the nearest secondary school or upgrade the village school to Class 10
Make the Class 8 examination harder so that fewer students pass
Close the village school and send all children to the city
Ask the students to walk 15 km each way to school

solution.concept: A course of action must remove the stated cause practically
solution.explanation: The stated cause of drop-outs is distance with no transport. Free transport, or classes up to 10 in the village, removes that cause directly.
steps: Problem: drop-outs after Class 8
Cause: secondary school 15 km away, no bus
Remedy: bring the school closer or provide transport
solution.why_others_wrong: A harder Class 8 exam pushes students out; closing the school or asking children to walk 30 km a day is impractical and harmful.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Provide free transport to the nearest secondary school or upgrade the village school to Class 10

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A shop sold 120 umbrellas in June and 300 umbrellas in July. The total number of items of all kinds that the shop sold in July was the same as in June.

Which of the following can be inferred?

options.text: It rained more in July than in June
The shop cut the price of umbrellas in July
The shop will sell more umbrellas in August than in July
Umbrellas made up a larger share of the items the shop sold in July than in June

solution.concept: Inference: only what the figures guarantee
solution.explanation: The total number of items sold was the same in both months, and umbrellas rose from 120 to 300, so umbrellas formed a larger share of the items sold in July.
steps: Same total in both months
Umbrellas: 120 → 300
So the umbrella share of the total rose
solution.why_others_wrong: Rain and a price cut are possible reasons that the data do not state; August sales are a prediction.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Umbrellas made up a larger share of the items the shop sold in July than in June

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city should make helmets compulsory for pillion riders on two-wheelers, because this will reduce deaths in two-wheeler accidents.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: In two-wheeler accidents in the city, pillion riders without helmets are four times as likely to die of head injuries as pillion riders wearing helmets
Helmets are now available in many colours and designs
Most two-wheeler riders in the city are below 40 years of age
Some pillion riders find helmets uncomfortable in summer

solution.concept: Strengthen: support the link between the proposal and the result
solution.explanation: The argument claims that helmets for pillion riders will reduce deaths. Evidence that unhelmeted pillion riders die far more often of head injuries directly supports that link.
steps: Claim: helmets for pillion riders → fewer deaths
Strengthener: evidence that helmets protect pillion riders in exactly such accidents
solution.why_others_wrong: Colours and the riders' age do not bear on deaths; discomfort, if anything, hints at lower compliance and slightly weakens the plan.
solution.final_answer: Option A: In two-wheeler accidents in the city, pillion riders without helmets are four times as likely to die of head injuries as pillion riders wearing helmets

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A café owner says that her new loyalty card has increased repeat visits, because repeat visits to the café rose by 15% in the three months after the card was launched.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens her claim?

options.text: A large office complex opened next to the café during the same three months, and most of the new repeat customers work there
The loyalty card is given free to every customer
Repeat visits at other cafés in the area fell during the same three months
The café also sells packaged snacks

solution.concept: Weaken a causal claim: another cause for the same effect
solution.explanation: If a new office complex next door brought in most of the new regular customers, the rise in repeat visits may be due to the office crowd, not the card.
steps: Claim: card → more repeat visits
Alternative cause in the same period: a new office complex next door
So the rise need not be due to the card
solution.why_others_wrong: A free card does not affect the causal claim; falling visits at other cafés actually support it; snack sales are irrelevant.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A large office complex opened next to the café during the same three months, and most of the new repeat customers work there

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a district, 60% of the households have an account in a public sector bank and 50% have an account in a private bank.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Exactly 10% of the households have accounts in both kinds of bank
40% of the households have an account only in a private bank
Public sector banks serve their customers better than private banks
At least 10% of the households have accounts in both a public sector bank and a private bank

solution.concept: Overlap of two groups: the minimum overlap is the excess over 100%
solution.explanation: 60% + 50% = 110%, which is more than 100%, so at least 10% of the households must be counted in both groups. The overlap could be larger (up to 50%), so 'exactly 10%' is not certain.
steps: Public + private = 110% of households
Since at most 100% of households exist, overlap ≥ 110% − 100% = 10%
The overlap can be anything from 10% to 50%
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Exactly 10%' would need every household to have at least one account, which is not stated; the 'only private' share cannot be fixed; the quality claim is not about the numbers at all.
solution.final_answer: Option D: At least 10% of the households have accounts in both a public sector bank and a private bank

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A bank has found that many of its elderly customers are being cheated by callers who pretend to be bank officials and persuade them to share the one-time passwords (OTPs) sent to their phones.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action for the bank?

options.text: Stop sending OTPs to customers above 60 years of age
Close the accounts of customers who have shared their OTPs
Stop all phone banking services for every customer
Run awareness drives for elderly customers, by branch meetings and messages, stating that the bank never asks for an OTP over the phone

solution.concept: A course of action should target the cause without harming customers
solution.explanation: The fraud works because elderly customers believe the callers. Teaching them that the bank never asks for an OTP attacks that cause directly and costs them nothing.
steps: Problem: elderly customers share OTPs with fake callers
Cause: they trust callers claiming to be the bank
Remedy: awareness that the bank never asks for OTPs
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping OTPs removes a security layer; closing victims' accounts punishes them; ending phone banking for all is an extreme step that does not address the deception.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Run awareness drives for elderly customers, by branch meetings and messages, stating that the bank never asks for an OTP over the phone

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Students who attend the school's optional evening classes score higher in the board examinations than those who do not. So the evening classes improve students' scores.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.text: Only students who were already among the top scorers of the school are allowed to join the evening classes
The evening classes are taken by the same teachers who teach the regular classes
Some students find the evening classes tiring
The board examination this year was equally difficult for all students

solution.concept: Weaken: show that the groups differed before the cause acted
solution.explanation: If only students who already scored high may join, their higher board scores can be explained by who joined, not by the classes. The argument's comparison then proves nothing about the classes' effect.
steps: Claim: evening classes → higher scores
Weakener: the class takes only students who were already top scorers (selection, not effect)
solution.why_others_wrong: Same teachers and equal difficulty do not explain the score gap; tiredness is irrelevant to the observed difference.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only students who were already among the top scorers of the school are allowed to join the evening classes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A city's bus company introduced air-conditioned buses on some routes. Over the next year, ridership on those routes rose by 25%, while ridership on the other routes did not change. During the same year, fares on all routes were raised by the same amount.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: Ridership on the routes with air-conditioned buses rose even though fares on those routes went up
Air-conditioning alone caused the rise in ridership on those routes
All the city's bus routes should be given air-conditioned buses
Ridership on the routes without air-conditioned buses fell

solution.concept: Inference: restate what the passage guarantees
solution.explanation: Fares rose on all routes, including those with the new buses, and ridership on those routes still rose by 25%. That is a direct combination of two stated facts.
steps: Fares rose on every route
Ridership on the air-conditioned routes rose 25%
⇒ the rise happened despite the fare increase
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage shows an association, not that air-conditioning alone caused it; a recommendation is not an inference; ridership on the other routes did not change.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Ridership on the routes with air-conditioned buses rose even though fares on those routes went up

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A hospital claims that its new appointment app has reduced the time patients wait at its outpatient department.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

options.text: Thousands of patients have downloaded the app
The number of outpatients and the number of doctors on duty were the same before and after the app was introduced, while the average waiting time fell from 90 minutes to 35 minutes
The app was developed by a well-known software firm
Waiting times also fell at nearby hospitals that do not use the app

solution.concept: Strengthen: rule out other explanations
solution.explanation: With patient numbers and doctors unchanged, the large fall in waiting time cannot be explained by fewer patients or more doctors, which supports the app as the cause.
steps: Claim: app → shorter waits
Strengthener: the main alternative causes (load, staffing) did not change while waits fell
solution.why_others_wrong: Downloads and the developer's name say nothing about waiting times; falling waits at hospitals without the app point to some other cause and weaken the claim.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The number of outpatients and the number of doctors on duty were the same before and after the app was introduced, while the average waiting time fell from 90 minutes to 35 minutes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Since the state lowered the speed limit on its expressway from 120 km/h to 100 km/h last year, the number of fatal accidents on the expressway has fallen by 30%. So the lower speed limit has made the expressway safer.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Before the change, most fatal accidents on the expressway involved vehicles driving above 100 km/h
The expressway is about 300 km long and has six lanes
For four months of the year since the limit was lowered, half of the expressway was closed for repairs, and traffic on it was about half the usual level
Many drivers complained that the lower limit increases their travel time

solution.concept: Weaken: an alternative explanation for the drop
solution.explanation: Far fewer vehicles on a partly closed road would by itself mean fewer accidents. The 30% fall may then reflect lower traffic, not the speed limit, so the conclusion is undermined.
steps: Conclusion: lower limit → fewer fatal accidents
Alternative: much lower traffic during repairs in the same period
The fall could be due to less traffic, not slower traffic
solution.why_others_wrong: Speeding being behind most earlier accidents supports the argument; road length is irrelevant; complaints about travel time do not bear on safety.
solution.final_answer: Option C: For four months of the year since the limit was lowered, half of the expressway was closed for repairs, and traffic on it was about half the usual level

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every customer of Bank X who has a credit card also has a savings account. Some customers who have savings accounts also have fixed deposits. No customer who has a fixed deposit has a home loan.

Which of the following must be true about the customers of Bank X?

options.text: Some customers who have credit cards also have fixed deposits
No customer who has a credit card has a home loan
Every customer who has a savings account has a credit card
No customer who has a home loan has a fixed deposit

solution.concept: Must-be-true: use only the definite statements
solution.explanation: 'No fixed-deposit holder has a home loan' means the two groups do not overlap, which can be stated from either side: no home-loan holder has a fixed deposit.
steps: No FD holder has a home loan ⇔ no home-loan holder has an FD
Credit-card holders ⊂ savings holders; the FD overlap is with 'some' savings holders only
solution.why_others_wrong: Credit-card holders may or may not have fixed deposits or home loans (only some savings holders have FDs); 'All credit-card holders have savings accounts' does not reverse.
solution.final_answer: Option D: No customer who has a home loan has a fixed deposit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Inspections have found that several private ambulance operators in the city charge patients' families far more than the usual rate in emergencies.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Fix and publish the maximum ambulance charge per kilometre, and penalise operators who charge more
Ban all private ambulances in the city
Advise families to bargain with the operator before putting the patient in the ambulance
Take no action, since ambulances are needed in emergencies

solution.concept: A course of action should be practical, proportionate and aimed at the problem
solution.explanation: The problem is overcharging. A published price cap with penalties stops it while keeping private ambulances available.
steps: Problem: overcharging in emergencies
Remedy: a transparent cap plus enforcement
Keeps the service running
solution.why_others_wrong: A total ban would leave patients without ambulances; bargaining in an emergency is impractical; doing nothing leaves the problem unsolved.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Fix and publish the maximum ambulance charge per kilometre, and penalise operators who charge more

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Our branch received 80 customer complaints last quarter and only 20 this quarter. So our customers are now much more satisfied with our service.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The branch hired two new staff members this quarter
This quarter the branch removed its complaint register and stopped accepting written complaints at the counter
Complaints at other branches of the bank rose this quarter
Most complaints last quarter were about the branch's air-conditioning

solution.concept: Weaken: attack the assumption that fewer recorded complaints means fewer unhappy customers
solution.explanation: The argument assumes that the number of recorded complaints reflects customer satisfaction. If the branch made complaining harder, the fall in complaints says little about satisfaction.
steps: Evidence: recorded complaints fell 80 → 20
Hidden assumption: recorded complaints track satisfaction
Removing the complaint channel breaks that assumption
solution.why_others_wrong: New staff could explain better service (it does not weaken); other branches' complaints are irrelevant; the topic of last quarter's complaints does not affect the comparison.
solution.final_answer: Option B: This quarter the branch removed its complaint register and stopped accepting written complaints at the counter

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city plans to build cycle lanes along its main roads, claiming that this will reduce car traffic on those roads.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

options.text: Cycling is a healthy form of exercise
The price of bicycles in the city has fallen this year
On two main roads where cycle lanes were built as a trial, car traffic fell by 18%, while it stayed the same on similar roads without cycle lanes
Some shopkeepers on the main roads oppose the cycle lanes

solution.concept: Strengthen: a controlled comparison
solution.explanation: A trial where car traffic fell on roads with lanes but not on similar roads without them is direct evidence that the lanes reduce car traffic.
steps: Claim: cycle lanes → less car traffic
Trial vs comparable roads isolates the effect of the lanes
solution.why_others_wrong: Health benefits and bicycle prices do not show any effect on car traffic; shopkeepers' opposition is irrelevant to the claim.
solution.final_answer: Option C: On two main roads where cycle lanes were built as a trial, car traffic fell by 18%, while it stayed the same on similar roads without cycle lanes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A company has 100 employees, 40 of whom work in Sales. This year, the average salary of the Sales employees rose by 10%, and the number of Sales employees did not change. The total salary paid to all 100 employees also rose by exactly 10%, and the number of employees outside Sales did not change either.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Every Sales employee received a 10% raise
The average salary outside Sales is the same as the average salary in Sales
No employee of the company had a salary cut this year
The total salary paid to the 60 employees outside Sales rose by exactly 10%

solution.concept: Totals rising by the same percentage force the remainder to rise by that percentage
solution.explanation: Let the old totals be T (company) and S (Sales). New totals are 1.1T and 1.1S (same staff, average up 10%). The rest of the company then gets 1.1T − 1.1S = 1.1(T − S): exactly 10% more than before.
steps: Sales total: S → 1.1S (40 employees, average +10%)
Company total: T → 1.1T
solution.why_others_wrong: A 10% rise in the average allows uneven individual raises; the two averages need not be equal; individual salaries could still fall while totals rise.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The total salary paid to the 60 employees outside Sales rose by exactly 10%
